subject: Quantitative Aptitude
description: Conditional probability, complement, addition rule, dice/cards, expected value

questions.stem: A bag has 5 red and 3 blue balls. The probability that a randomly drawn ball is BLUE is:

options.option_text: 5/8 (the red fraction)
3/8 (the blue fraction)
1/2 (assumes equal split)
3/5 (blue divided by red)

questions.explanation: P(blue) = blue / total = 3 / (5+3) = 3/8. Distractor 1 swaps numerator (gives red probability). Distractor 3 ignores the actual counts. Distractor 4 uses the wrong denominator (just red).
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.stem: Two dice are tossed together. The probability that the SUM is 7 is:

options.option_text: 5/36 (one fewer than the actual count)
6/36 = 1/6 (six favourable pairs)
7/36 (taken from the sum value)
1/12 (half of the correct value)

questions.explanation: Total outcomes = 6×6 = 36. Pairs giving sum 7: (1,6),(2,5),(3,4),(4,3),(5,2),(6,1) = 6 pairs. P = 6/36 = 1/6. Sum 7 is the most likely outcome with two fair dice. Distractor 1 = 5/36 (sum 6 or 8). Distractor 3 = 7/36 (no valid pairing). Distractor 4 = halves the answer.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.stem: From a pack of 52 cards, the probability of drawing a KING is:

options.option_text: 1/52 (a single specified card)
1/13 (any one of four kings)
1/4 (any one of four suits)
3/13 (any J, Q or K card)

questions.explanation: 4 kings (one per suit) in 52 cards. P = 4/52 = 1/13. Distractor 1 — single card. Distractor 3 = 13/52 = 1/4 (any suit). Distractor 4 = 12/52 = 3/13 (any face card: J, Q, K).
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.stem: If P(A) = 0.4 and P(B) = 0.5 and the events are MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE, then P(A or B) =

options.option_text: 0.2 (the product of probabilities)
0.9 (the sum of probabilities)
0.7 (an arbitrary combined value)
0.5 (the larger of the two)

questions.explanation: Mutually exclusive: P(A and B) = 0. So P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) = 0.4 + 0.5 = 0.9. Distractor 1 = product (gives joint probability of INDEPENDENT events, not 'or'). Distractor 3 from arbitrary combination. Distractor 4 ignores the additive rule.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.stem: A coin is tossed 3 times. The probability of getting EXACTLY 2 heads is:

options.option_text: 1/4 (random guess)
3/8 (correct binomial value)
1/2 (half because equal heads/tails)
1/8 (one specific sequence only)

questions.explanation: 3 tosses: 2³ = 8 equally likely outcomes. Exactly 2 heads can occur in C(3,2) = 3 ways: HHT, HTH, THH. P = 3/8. Binomial: P = C(3,2) × (1/2)² × (1/2)¹ = 3 × 1/8 = 3/8. Distractor 1 = 1/4 random guess. Distractor 3 = 1/2 confused with at-least-1-head. Distractor 4 = 1/8 (probability of one specific outcome).
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.stem: The probability of an event A NOT occurring equals:

options.option_text: 1 + P(A) (sum greater than 1)
1 − P(A) (the complement rule)
P(A) ÷ 2 (an arbitrary halving)
P(A) × 0 (yields zero always)

questions.explanation: Complement Rule: P(not A) = 1 − P(A). Total probability is 1; everything not-A is the rest. Useful for 'at least one' problems: P(at least 1) = 1 − P(none). Distractor 1 — sum exceeds 1, impossible for valid probability. Distractor 3 — arbitrary. Distractor 4 — would always give zero.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.stem: Two cards are drawn at random WITHOUT REPLACEMENT from a standard deck of 52. The probability that BOTH are aces is:

options.option_text: 1/169 (independent multiplication)
1/221 (correct dependent value)
4/52 (one ace probability)
1/52 (a single ace fraction)

questions.explanation: Without replacement: P(1st ace) = 4/52 = 1/13. P(2nd ace given 1st was ace) = 3/51 = 1/17. P(both) = 1/13 × 1/17 = 1/221. Distractor 1 = (4/52)² = 1/169 (independent multiplication, valid only WITH replacement). Distractor 3 = single-ace probability. Distractor 4 from another wrong reading.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.stem: A box contains 6 white and 4 black marbles. Two marbles are drawn one by one WITH replacement. What is the probability that both drawn marbles are white?

options.option_text: 9/25, since each independent draw gives P(white) = 3/5
3/5, the probability of drawing one white marble only
1/3, the probability computed without replacement instead
6/25, treating the second draw as having different odds

questions.explanation: With replacement, each draw is independent. P(white) = 6/10 = 3/5 each time. P(both white) = (3/5) × (3/5) = 9/25. Option C (1/3) is the without-replacement answer: C(6,2)/C(10,2) = 15/45 = 1/3 — a frequent error when candidates ignore the 'with replacement' condition.

questions.stem: The letters of the word 'MOBILE' are arranged at random. What is the probability that all three vowels (O, I, E) always appear together?

options.option_text: 1/5, by treating all three vowels as a single unit block
1/6, since 3 vowels out of 6 letters gives a direct ratio
1/20, placing vowels in 3 specific fixed positions only
3/10, by partial permutation over only the three vowel slots

questions.explanation: Treat OIE as one block → 4 units (block + M, B, L). Arrangements = 4! × 3! = 24 × 6 = 144. Total = 6! = 720. P = 144/720 = 1/5. Option B (1/6) is wrong — it naively uses the vowel count as a denominator without accounting for internal rearrangements and block-grouping logic.

questions.stem: Three students A, B, and C independently attempt to solve a puzzle. Their probabilities of success are 1/3, 2/5, and 1/2 respectively. What is the probability that at least one of them solves the puzzle?

options.option_text: 4/5, using the complement: 1 minus P(none of them succeeds)
37/30, the direct sum of all three probabilities combined
3/5, treating only A's failure as the complementary event
2/15, multiplying all three success probabilities together

questions.explanation: P(none succeeds) = (1 − 1/3)(1 − 2/5)(1 − 1/2) = (2/3)(3/5)(1/2) = 6/30 = 1/5. So P(at least one) = 1 − 1/5 = 4/5. Option D (2/15) is the joint probability that ALL three succeed — the most common mix-up between 'at least one' and 'all' in multi-event problems.

questions.stem: In a class of 30 students, 12 play cricket, 10 play football, and 5 play both. A student is chosen at random. What is the probability that the student plays cricket but NOT football?

options.option_text: 7/30, subtracting dual-sport students from the cricket count
2/5, using the full cricket count of 12 without adjustment
17/30, adding cricket and football totals and dividing by 30
1/6, treating only the 5 dual-sport students as the answer

questions.explanation: Cricket only = 12 − 5 = 7 (removing those who also play football). P = 7/30. Option B (2/5 = 12/30) ignores the overlap, counting dual-sport students in the cricket group — the classic set-theory error of not applying the 'but not' condition.

questions.stem: Two fair dice are rolled. Given that the sum of the two dice is even, what is the probability that both dice show the same number?

options.option_text: 1/3, since all six doubles produce an even sum guaranteed
1/6, the unconditioned probability of any double over 36 outcomes
1/2, since even-sum outcomes are exactly half of all 36 results
2/9, counting doubles only among the 9 both-even outcomes

questions.explanation: Even sum occurs when both dice are even (9 outcomes) or both odd (9 outcomes) → 18 total. All six doubles (1,1)...(6,6) yield even sums → 6 favorable. P = 6/18 = 1/3. Option B (1/6) is P(double) without the given condition — it ignores the conditional restriction to even-sum outcomes entirely.

questions.stem: Machines A, B, and C produce 40%, 35%, and 25% of a factory's output with defect rates of 2%, 3%, and 4% respectively. A randomly picked item is defective. What is the probability it came from machine B?

options.option_text: 7/19, applying Bayes' theorem to the weighted defect contributions
7/20, using B's 35% production share as a direct probability
1/3, dividing B's defect rate by the simple sum of all three rates
21/100, multiplying B's share and defect rate without normalising

questions.explanation: P(defective) = 0.40×0.02 + 0.35×0.03 + 0.25×0.04 = 0.008 + 0.0105 + 0.010 = 0.0285. By Bayes: P(B | defective) = (0.35×0.03)/0.0285 = 0.0105/0.0285 = 105/285 = 7/19 ≈ 0.368. Option D (21/100 = 0.21) is the un-normalised numerator alone — the hallmark error of skipping the total-probability denominator in Bayes problems.

questions.stem: A player rolls a fair die once. If the outcome is even, the player wins ₹ equal to the face value. If the outcome is odd, the player loses ₹ equal to (face value − 1). What is the player's expected gain per game?

options.option_text: ₹1 per game, as the net across all six equiprobable outcomes is ₹6
₹0 per game, since the game appears symmetric and balanced overall
₹2 per game, summing only even-outcome gains and dividing by 3
₹0.50 per game, averaging the win range and loss range without 1/6 weight

questions.explanation: Even outcomes: win ₹2, ₹4, ₹6. Odd outcomes: lose ₹(1−1)=0, ₹(3−1)=2, ₹(5−1)=4. E = (1/6)(+2+4+6−0−2−4) = (1/6)(6) = ₹1. Option B (₹0) is the intuitive but wrong 'symmetric game' assumption — the asymmetry arises because odd face-value 1 costs nothing while even face-value 2 pays ₹2, breaking symmetry in the player's favour.
